title: Loading related data
summary: Include and ThenInclude, filtered includes, explicit loading, and why lazy loading is risky.

steps.title: Eager loading with Include
body: A query loads only the entity you asked for. To bring related data **in the same query**, ask for it with `Include`:
The SQL joins the two tables:
This is **eager loading**: you say up front what you will need. Go deeper with `ThenInclude`:
and filter or sort the included collection right inside `Include` (a **filtered include**):

code: seed.Authors.Add(new Author { Name = "Le Guin", Books = [new() { Title = "Earthsea" }, new() { Title = "The Dispossessed" }] });
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: Without `Include`, `Books` is just the empty list the class starts with: nothing was loaded. With it, both of Le Guin's books arrive in the same query.

steps.prompt: Arrange the query: authors, with their books, with each book's reviews, ordered by author name.
steps.explain: `ThenInclude` continues from the navigation just included, so it must follow its `Include`. Sorting comes before running the query with `ToList`.

steps.title: Explicit loading
body: Sometimes you only discover later that you need related data, and only for some entities. **Explicit loading** fetches a navigation of an entity you already have:
db.Entry(book).Reference(b => b.Author).Load();             // for a reference navigation
You can also query a navigation without loading it all:
var count = db.Entry(author).Collection(a => a.Books).Query().Count();   // SELECT COUNT(*)

code: seed.Authors.Add(new Author { Name = "Le Guin", Books = [new() { Title = "Earthsea" }, new() { Title = "The Dispossessed" }] });
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db");
steps.explain: `Load` fills the navigation. `Query().Count()` only counts in the database, so `leGuin.Books` stays empty: nothing was loaded into it.

steps.title: Lazy loading, and why it is risky
body: **Lazy loading** loads a navigation automatically the first time you touch it. It needs the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Proxies` package, `options.UseLazyLoadingProxies()`, and `virtual` navigations:
It looks convenient, and that is the danger:
- **Hidden queries.** Nothing in the code says "database". A loop over 500 authors runs 501 queries: the **N+1 problem** (module 7).
- **Surprises after the context is gone.** Touch a navigation after the context is disposed (in a JSON serializer, say) and it throws, or serializing walks your whole database.
- **Hard to review.** You cannot see what a method costs by reading it.
Most teams leave lazy loading off and use `Include` or projections (module 4). This course does not ship the proxies package; you will see the same N+1 effect with explicit code instead.

steps.prompt: A page shows 50 orders with the customer name of each. Lazy loading is on, and the code loops over `db.Orders.Take(50).ToList()` reading `order.Customer.Name`. How many queries run?
options: Up to 51: one for the orders, one per order for its customer
2: one for orders, one for all customers
steps.explain: Each first touch of `order.Customer` triggers its own query (the same customer is only loaded once, so it is *up to* 51). `Include(o => o.Customer)` would make it one query.

steps.prompt: Match each loading strategy to its description.
pairs: `Include` in the query: related data comes in the same round trip
Touching the navigation runs a query behind your back
`Select` only the related fields you need into a new shape
steps.explain: Eager and explicit loading make every query visible in your code; lazy loading hides them. Projections, coming in module 4, are often the best of all.

steps.title: A reading report
prompt: The tests give you the model below. Write `List<string> Report(LibraryDb db)` that returns, for every author **ordered by name**, a line like

listing the author's books ordered by title, each with its number of reviews. An author without books prints `Name:` with nothing after the colon. Load the data with **one** query using `Include` and `ThenInclude`.
class Author { public int Id; public string Name; public List<Book> Books; }
class Book   { public int Id; public string Title; public int AuthorId; public Author Author; public List<Review> Reviews; }
class Review { public int Id; public int Stars; public int BookId; public Book Book; }
template: dojoDb.Authors.Add(new Author { Name = "Le Guin", Books = [new() { Title = "The Dispossessed" }, new() { Title = "Earthsea", Reviews = [new() { Stars = 5 }, new() { Stars = 4 }] }] });
dojoDb.Authors.Add(new Author { Name = "Herbert", Books = [new() { Title = "Dune", Reviews = [new() { Stars = 5 }] }] });
Dojo.Eq("the report", new List<string> { "Austen:", "Herbert: Dune (1)", "Le Guin: Earthsea (2), The Dispossessed (0)" }, dojoLines);
public Author Author { get; set; } = null!;
public Book Book { get; set; } = null!;
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=report.db")
hints: `Include(a => a.Books.OrderBy(b => b.Title)).ThenInclude(b => b.Reviews)` loads everything at once.
After `ToList()`, build the strings in memory with `Select` and `string.Join`.
